bridge: From A02, state the exact security property and the assumptions a proof would need. From P05, a test checks selected concrete inputs; from M02, express the conditions for a path; from F02, explain the limits of a mitigation; from M05, distinguish a sample from a whole population. This lesson compares what finite tests and analyses can establish against the stated property. Use the supplied parser and test inputs; no external service is needed.
teaching:
In ordinary testing you choose a concrete input such as "2:ab" and observe one run. Symbolic execution instead uses a placeholder such as x and records the conditions needed to follow each branch. A path constraint is that accumulated list of conditions. Fuzzing chooses many concrete inputs; static analysis reasons about code without running each input. These methods answer overlapping questions with different limits.

Fuzzing explores inputs automatically within a generation strategy and budget. A crash is a concrete finding; no crash in a finite set is not proof of absence. Static analysis reasons from code without executing each concrete input, while symbolic execution tracks path constraints and tries to solve for inputs that reach a branch.

Use a tiny parser so every input and failure can be inspected. Define expected handling of malformed input, not just valid examples. Unexpected exception types can reveal an unchecked assumption. Minimise a failure by removing bytes while keeping the same property failure, then add a regression test.

Coverage counts depend on the instrument and objective. Executing every line does not establish every state, schedule or business property. Record generator, bounds and seed where randomness exists. This deterministic enumeration requires no random seed and makes its exact workload visible.

A symbolic state maps variables to expressions and tracks the conditions under which control reaches them. For t=max(x,y), one branch has x>y and t=x; the other has x<=y and t=y. Adding the failure condition t<x contradicts either branch, so this model cannot reach that failure. This conclusion uses the exact comparison/assignment semantics. Introducing overflow-prone arithmetic, external calls, aliases or a different integer model requires additional reasoning. A solver timeout or an unexplored loop is unresolved, not safe.

One complete repair under an explicit ASCII-only grammar is:

```python
def parse_count(text):
    if not isinstance(text, str) or len(text) < 3:
        raise ValueError("shape")
    if text[0] not in "123456789" or text[1] != ":":
        raise ValueError("prefix")
    body = text[2:]
    if len(body) != int(text[0]) or not all(
        "a" <= ch <= "z" or "A" <= ch <= "Z" for ch in body
    ):
        raise ValueError("body")
    return body
```

This policy permits 1–9 ASCII letters, rejects 0: and makes a Unicode-letter choice explicit. It is not a claim about a future expanded grammar. Trace it against the seven fixture inputs before adding any new cases.
explanation: The empty string and "1" reach unchecked indexing. A repair checks shape/length before indexing, validates a single ASCII digit and separator, then validates body length/letters. Decide whether zero-length bodies are allowed: this fixture requires at least one letter, so "0:" rejects.
exercise: Without external tools, trace all seven supplied inputs and classify accepted, expected ValueError or unexpected exception. Write a guarded repair and assert the intended outcomes. Do not launch any evaluation or model inference as part of this exercise.
solution: The original parser accepts "1:a" and "2:ab". The empty string and input "1" raise IndexError. Inputs "2:a", "x:a" and "1;a" raise ValueError. The repaired parser rejects every malformed case with the documented validation error and preserves both valid cases.
challenge: Compare two finite input sets: A=["1:a","2:ab"], B=the seven supplied cases. State the extra defects B reveals and a property neither set proves. Write path constraints for the successful n=2 branch.
challenge_solution: B exposes missing length guards. Neither proves all Unicode, resource-limit or future grammar properties. Successful n=2 requires adequate length, first digit 2, colon at index 1, exactly 2 body characters and the stated alphabet rule. Define whether ASCII-only or Unicode letters are intended.
